resources.string: The variation in time between successive heartbeats (RMSSD), a window on the nervous system that steers recovery. The watch measures it in five-minute windows while you sleep; the night\'s value is their median, as Fitbit reports it. With the Google Health API connected (Settings, Data sources), the night takes Fitbit\'s own nightly value instead, so both apps agree. Otherwise, when Fitbit shares the values for less than 60 % of the time asleep, the night has none rather than a wrong one.\n\nHRV differs a lot between people, so it is judged against your own nights: your range is where 80 % of the nights in the 60 days before fell (10th to 90th percentile). Lower than usual often follows hard training, illness, alcohol, stress or short sleep; higher than usual usually means good recovery. Readiness judges a recent average of the last seven nights, the latest counting most, against a narrower band: the smallest change worth noticing (Plews 2013).

The heart rate the watch derives from the night, a steady measure of how hard the heart works at rest. Your range is where 80 % of the 30 nights before fell, at least 2 bpm either side of the usual value because the watch reports whole beats.\n\nA few beats above usual can follow hard training, illness, alcohol, heat or poor sleep. A lower resting heart rate over months is one sign of improving aerobic fitness.

Breaths per minute during sleep, as Fitbit reports it for the night. It is one of the steadiest measures the watch takes; your range is where 80 % of the 30 nights before fell, at least half a breath either side of the usual value.\n\nA rise of a breath or more above usual, with lower HRV or a higher resting heart rate, is a common early sign of illness, which is why readiness takes it into account.

The lowest heart rate of the night, from five-minute averages. It is often well below the resting heart rate Fitbit reports, which describes the night as a whole. Your range is where 80 % of the 30 nights before fell, at least 2 bpm either side of the usual value.
Readiness, %1$s, on the levels take it easy, train with care and ready to train
Provisional: the HRV baseline has fewer than 14 nights
Breathing raised: held at 40 or below

How ready your body is to train today, as a score from 0 to 100, from what the watch measured overnight and from recent training, each against your own normal: HRV\'s recent average, the last seven nights with the latest counting most (35 %), last night\'s sleep (25 %), resting heart rate (20 %) and form (20 %). Each part moves the score by its weight, and a part without data leaves its weight to the others. The one exception is illness: raised breathing together with low HRV or a raised resting heart rate holds the score at 40 or below.\n\nFrom 70 the body is ready for hard training; below 50 an easy day is usually the better choice. The score is a guide, not an instruction: how you feel counts too.
No heart rate from the watch on this day.
Heart rate over the day, from %1$d to %2$d beats a minute

All-day heart rate as the watch recorded it, read from Health Connect when you open this page rather than stored. The watch\'s app passes heart rate on when it syncs with the watch, so today\'s line can stop some minutes before now.\n\nThe line is coloured by your heart rate zones, anchored on your threshold heart rate; touch it to read a time. Resting heart rate is the watch\'s value for the night that ended on this day.

The average share of haemoglobin carrying oxygen (SpO2) over the night, which the watch estimates from red and infrared light at the wrist. Fitbit computes it and shares it through the Google Health API; Health Connect does not carry it.
Awake at sea level, healthy values are 95 % or above, and they run a little lower in sleep. A wrist estimate is less exact than a fingertip oximeter, so compare nights with your own range: where 80 % of the 30 nights before fell, at least half a point either side of the usual value. Several low nights in a row can come with illness, altitude or disturbed breathing in sleep.

Skin temperature at the wrist during sleep, as the difference from Fitbit\'s own baseline for you. Fitbit computes it and shares it through the Google Health API; Health Connect does not carry it.
Skin temperature follows the room and the bedding as well as the body, so single nights move by a few tenths of a degree. A rise that lasts several nights often comes with illness, and in women it follows the menstrual cycle. Your range is where 80 % of the 30 nights before fell, at least 0.2 °C either side of the usual value.
The alertness score of each of the last 30 days, on the bands of alert, reduced and low

For three minutes a counter starts in the box at random moments. Tap anywhere on the screen as soon as it starts; the time you took shows for a second. A tap before the counter starts is a false start.\n\nTake it the same way each time: seated, the phone in the same hand, notifications out of the way. Tests at different times of day teach the model the most. Leaving the screen stops the test, since only the full three minutes count.

Your first tests set your own speed; comparisons with the model start from the third.
Lapses are answers of half a second or slower. The reaction time is 1000 divided by your mean response speed, so a few slow answers do not dominate it.

# HRV
The line is the recent average of the last seven days (at least 3 nights), with $h = \ln \mathrm{RMSSD}$ and the night $k$ days ago weighted $7 - k$:

$$\bar{h}_r = \frac{\sum_k (7 - k)\, h_k}{\sum_k (7 - k)}$$

$$\mathrm{line} = e^{\bar{h}_r}$$

The band on each day comes from the 60 days before its last seven (at least 7 nights), with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $s$:

$$e^{\mu - s/2} \;\text{ to }\; e^{\mu + s/2}$$

The 7-day variation is the coefficient of variation of $h$ over the week (at least 5 nights), in per cent:

$$\mathrm{CV}_7 = 100\, \frac{\operatorname{sd}(h)}{\bar{h}}$$

with its usual range the 10th to 90th percentile of the weekly values of the previous 60 days (at least 14 of them).

# Resting heart rate
The line is the mean of the last seven days (at least 3 nights). The band is the 10th to 90th percentile of the 30 nights before, at least 2 bpm either side of their median. Before 14 nights, with the mean $\bar{r}$ and standard deviation $s_r$ of the nights before:

$$\bar{r} \pm \max(s_r,\; 3\,\mathrm{bpm})$$
Nightly HRV with its recent average, the latest nights weighted most, and normal range

How your body handles training over weeks and months, measured each night. HRV and resting heart rate react to training, illness and stress, so their trends show whether recovery keeps up with the work.

# Reading the charts
- Dots are single nights. The HRV line is its recent average, the one readiness judges; the resting heart rate line is the average of the last seven nights.
- The shaded band is your own normal range on each day; it moves as your baseline does. For HRV it is the band readiness holds the recent average against; for resting heart rate the range a single night usually falls in, as on the Today tile.
- The line turns orange while it sits outside the band.

# HRV
The normal range is the mean of the 60 days before the last week, plus or minus half a standard deviation, on the log scale (Plews 2013); the week being judged is left out of it. The recent average covers the last seven nights and weights last night seven times, the night before six times, down to once a week back, so good nights after a poor spell show as recovery within days. A recent average below the range is the clearest sign of accumulated fatigue, illness or stress; a rising range over months often comes with better fitness.

The 7-day variation is the coefficient of variation of ln HRV over the week (Plews 2012; HRV4Training shows it the same way), with your usual range from the previous 60 days. A steady mean with rising variation points to a disturbed balance: hard training, illness or travel. In elite triathletes a falling mean with shrinking variation came before non-functional overreaching (Plews 2012), so read it together with the mean.

# Resting heart rate
The usual range is where 80 % of the 30 nights before fell, at least 2 bpm either side of their median; with fewer than 14 nights, your average plus or minus one standard deviation, at least 3 bpm. A raised resting heart rate for several nights points the same way as low HRV.

A range appears after a week of nights for resting heart rate and two weeks for HRV, whose band leaves out the last week.
Nightly resting heart rate with its seven-day average and usual range

# Still minutes
A minute $m$ is still when it has at least 3 heart rate samples, no steps from $m - 5$ to $m$, lies outside sleep records and workouts (from 5 minutes before to 60 after, or 15 after a detected walk or ride), and its mean heart rate $h_m \le 130$.

# Hourly usual
For hour $k$ of day $d$, with $\bar{h}_{k,d'}$ the mean still heart rate of hour $k$ on an earlier day $d'$ (with at least 10 still minutes in that hour), from at least 7 days:

$$u_{k,d} = \operatorname*{median}_{d - 28 \le d' < d} \bar{h}_{k,d'}$$

# Excess
With $n_{k,d}$ the still minutes of hour $k$, over the hours that have a usual and from 120 still minutes:

$$E_d = \frac{\sum_k n_{k,d}\, \left(\bar{h}_{k,d} - u_{k,d}\right)}{\sum_k n_{k,d}}$$

# Score
With $\tilde{E}$ the median of $E$ over the 28 days before and MAD its median absolute deviation (at least 14 days):

$$s = \max\left(1.4826\, \mathrm{MAD},\; 1.5\right)$$

$$S_d = 50 + 10\, \frac{E_d - \tilde{E}}{s}$$

clamped to 0 to 100: a T-score among your own days, made robust to odd days by the median and MAD.

# Other causes
- Vitals: two or more of HRV, resting heart rate, breathing rate, SpO2 and skin temperature outside their usual range on the morning of the day or the next.
- Hard training: a day's load $L_d \ge 60$ and $L_d \ge 1.5\, C_{d-1}$, with $C$ fitness, that day or the day before.
- Poor sleep: a sleep score under 65 the night before.
Daytime strain over the last four weeks
It comes once today has two hours of still, awake time away from workouts.

How much higher your heart rate ran than usual while you were still and awake: heart rate that movement does not explain. Physiologists call it additional heart rate and use it as a sign of emotional strain in daily life (Myrtek 2004). It is not a measure of how stressed you feel, and a watch cannot see cortisol.

# How it is worked out
- Still minutes: no steps on any device in that minute or the 5 before, not in bed, not during a workout or the hour after it (15 minutes after a detected walk or ride), and heart rate at most 130.
- Your usual: for each hour of the day, the median heart rate of your still minutes over the four weeks before, so that your daily rhythm and habits such as sitting at work are taken out.
- The day: how far its still minutes ran above those hourly usuals, in bpm, from two hours of still time.
- The score: 50 is a usual day for you, and every 10 points is one typical day-to-day spread above or below. Calm below 40, usual to 60, raised from 60, high from 70.
- Today counts so far and is read again every few minutes while the app is open.

# How far to trust it
Confidence is low to moderate, so it is marked experimental:
- In daily life, wrist heart rate measures explain only a few per cent of how stressed people say they feel (1 to 3 % in 657 people over eight weeks; JMIR Cardio 2021). In the lab, heart rate corrected for movement told mental from physical stress apart only weakly (van de Ven 2025).
- Much besides stress raises still heart rate: illness, heat, caffeine, alcohol the night before, a large meal, dehydration, short sleep, hard training and standing rather than sitting, which the watch cannot see. A ride without steps is left out only when an app detected it or heart rate went above 130.
- It describes your body, not your mind: a raised day means something put a load on it. Where your data shows one, the card names it: vitals off around that day (often an illness starting), hard training or a poor night.

# What it is good for
Spotting days and weeks when your body runs hotter than usual, and a factor in Sleep factors. Single days are noisy; a run of raised days says more.

It needs about three weeks of wearing the watch in the day: one for the hourly usuals, two more to set the scale.
It compares each day with your own usual days, so it needs three weeks of wearing the watch in the day.
